content: Breastfeeding involves feeding an infant or young child with breast milk directly from the mother's breasts, rather than using a bottle or other container. Infants are born with a natural sucking reflex that allows them to suck and swallow milk effectively. Most mothers are capable of exclusively breastfeeding their infants for the first six months of life without the need for supplemental formula or solid foods. According to a 2001 World Health Organization (WHO) report, alternatives to direct breastfeeding include expressed breast milk from the infant's own mother, breast milk from a healthy wet nurse or a human milk bank, or a breast milk substitute fed with a cup, which is considered safer than using a bottle and teat. Human breast milk is widely regarded as the optimal source of nutrition for infants, as it helps prevent diseases, promotes overall health, and reduces healthcare costs. However, there are exceptions, such as when the mother is taking certain medications or is infected with tuberculosis or HIV. Experts have differing opinions on the ideal duration of breastfeeding to maximize benefits and on the risks associated with using artificial formulas. In both developing and developed countries, formula feeding is linked to higher rates of infant mortality due to diarrhea. The WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life and continued breastfeeding for at least two years. Similarly, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) advises exclusive breastfeeding for six months and continued breastfeeding for at least one year. Exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months provides significant protection against diarrhea and respiratory tract infections, which are more common in formula-fed infants. Both the WHO and AAP emphasize the importance of breastfeeding for the health of both mothers and children. Lactation refers to the production, secretion, and ejection of milk, a defining characteristic of mammals. Breast milk is derived from nutrients in the mother's bloodstream and bodily stores. Studies estimate that exclusively breastfeeding mothers use an additional 400–600 calories per day to produce milk. The composition of breast milk changes based on the duration of nursing, with research showing that its fat and energy content increases after the first year. Breast milk adapts to meet the nutritional needs of a toddler's developing system, providing the right nutrients at the right time. For example, between 12 and 24 months, 448 milliliters of breast milk can provide significant percentages of a toddler's daily nutritional requirements, including 29% of energy, 76% of folate, 43% of protein, 94% of vitamin B12, 36% of calcium, 60% of vitamin C, and 75% of vitamin A. Breastfeeding offers numerous benefits for infants. Nutrients and antibodies are transferred to the baby, and the maternal bond is strengthened. Research has demonstrated various advantages, including a reduced risk of breast cancer in women who were breastfed as infants, prevention or delay of atopic syndrome in at-risk children through exclusive breastfeeding for four months, and a lower likelihood of developing atopic dermatitis with exclusive breastfeeding beyond 12 weeks in families with a history of atopy. Breastfeeding while introducing gluten to the diet has been associated with a reduced risk of celiac disease, though it is unclear whether this offers lifelong protection or merely delays symptoms. Exclusively breastfed infants have a lower risk of developing type 1 diabetes compared to those exposed to cow's milk and solid foods earlier. Breastfeeding also appears to protect against type 2 diabetes, partly due to its effects on the child's weight. Breastfeeding protects against diarrhea, with lower death rates from diarrhea in breastfed infants compared to formula-fed peers, regardless of the country's development level. Breast milk contains anti-infective factors such as bile salt-stimulated lipase, lactoferrin, and immunoglobulin A, which protect against infections. Despite being a potential factor in mother-to-child HIV transmission, certain components in breast milk, such as polyunsaturated fatty acids, may reduce the risk of infection and viral shedding. However, breastfeeding does not appear to protect against all allergies. Breastfeeding has been linked to higher intelligence in babies with a specific variant of the FADS2 gene, with an average IQ increase of seven points. It also reduces the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), particularly in premature infants, with formula-fed infants being six to ten times more likely to develop NEC. Breast milk contains the ideal ratio of amino acids to support the development of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Long-term cognitive benefits have been observed in children who were breastfed for more than eight months, particularly those born with low birth weight. Breastfeeding also reduces the risk of extreme obesity in children aged 39 to 42 months, with the protective effect increasing with the duration of breastfeeding. Breastfeeding reduces the duration of certain types of middle ear infections and lowers the risk of upper respiratory tract infections in premature infants up to seven months after hospital discharge. Breastfed babies have improved arousal from sleep, which may reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Breastfeeding also reduces the risk of urinary tract infections in infants up to seven months postpartum, with the strongest protection occurring immediately after birth. For mothers, breastfeeding is a cost-effective way to feed an infant and provides the best nourishment at a minimal nutrient cost to the mother. Frequent and exclusive breastfeeding can delay the return of fertility through lactational amenorrhea, though it is not a reliable method of birth control. Breastfeeding releases beneficial hormones like oxytocin and prolactin, which relax the mother and strengthen the maternal bond. Breastfeeding mothers have a reduced risk of endometrial, breast, and ovarian cancers, as well as osteoporosis. It also stabilizes maternal endometriosis, reduces the risk of postpartum bleeding, and benefits insulin levels in mothers with polycystic ovary syndrome. However, some mothers may experience pain from infections like candidiasis or staphylococcus, which can be managed with medical attention. Breastfeeding can help mothers lose weight as fat accumulated during pregnancy is used to produce milk, though weight loss varies among lactating women. Diet and exercise remain more reliable methods for weight loss. Breastfeeding soon after birth increases oxytocin levels, helping the uterus contract more quickly and reducing bleeding. Breastfeeding laws in many U.S. states allow mothers to breastfeed anywhere they are permitted to be. Rooming-in care in hospitals and breastfeeding rooms in public places support breastfeeding mothers. Breastfeeding difficulties are common but can often be resolved with proper hospital procedures, trained staff, and lactation consultants. Early breastfeeding within the first half-hour after birth is ideal, as the baby's sucking reflex is strongest. However, overfeeding may lead to an imbalance of foremilk and hindmilk, potentially causing problems. Proper latching techniques and comfortable positions are essential for effective breastfeeding. Expressing breast milk is an option when direct breastfeeding is not possible, and expressed milk can be stored for later use.
